title: Clear the bar or stay out
allegory: A JumpReLU latent is like a door with its own height bar: anyone below the bar stays out, anyone above walks in at full height, and the fee is per guest rather than per centimetre, so nobody is made to shrink.
map: the height bar, set separately for each door
below the bar: out; above it: in at full height
JumpReLU: 0 if z < θ, otherwise z itself (no shrinking)
a flat fee per guest, not per centimetre
an L0 penalty (how many latents fire) instead of L1 (how big they are)
guessing how to move the bar from guests who nearly made it
the straight-through estimator: a stand-in gradient near the threshold

chapters.name: The shrinking tax
chapters.note: L1: pay for every unit of loudness

cap.1: A sparse autoencoder is told to use few latents. The classic way taxes each latent by how strongly it fires, so even the real ones learn to whisper.
cap.2: A ReLU SAE with an L1 penalty pays for the size of every activation. Lowering all activations lowers the bill, so true feature strengths come out systematically too small: shrinkage.
cap.3: L1 sparsity biases active latents toward zero: the penalty's gradient λ·sign(f) pushes every active magnitude down regardless of reconstruction, so estimated feature strengths shrink.

cap.1: JumpReLU puts a height bar at each door. Below the bar, you stay out. Clear it, and you walk in at your full height. Each door learns where its own bar sits.
cap.2: Each latent has a learned threshold θ. If its pre-activation z is below θ the output is 0; above θ it passes z through unchanged. Small noisy activations are cut, real ones keep their size.
cap.3: JumpReLU_θ(z) = z · H(z − θ), with H the Heaviside step and θ > 0 learned per latent. Unlike ReLU(z − θ), it doesn't subtract θ, so active latents aren't shrunk.

cap.1: Flat at zero, then a sudden jump to the full value. Plain ReLU lets tiny values leak through; a shifted ReLU cuts them but shrinks the rest.
cap.2: Three ways to gate a latent. ReLU: anything positive counts, so small noise fires. ReLU(z − θ): noise is cut, but every real value loses θ. JumpReLU: noise cut, real values intact.
cap.3: JumpReLU is discontinuous at θ, trading a continuous activation for magnitude fidelity. That discontinuity is exactly why θ needs a special gradient estimator.

cap.1: Nudging the bar usually changes nothing, then suddenly lets someone in. No slope to learn from, so training uses a stand-in slope near the bar.
cap.2: H(z − θ) is 0 or 1, so its true gradient with respect to θ is zero almost everywhere. A straight-through estimator substitutes a pseudo-gradient that is non-zero only for z near θ.
cap.3: The STE replaces ∂H/∂θ with a narrow kernel around z = θ (its width is a bandwidth hyperparameter), so the losses can move each threshold. The same trick makes an L0 penalty trainable.

chapters.name: Pay per guest
chapters.verdict: Charge for showing up, not for how loud you are.

cap.1: The fee changes too. Instead of paying for how loud each latent is, you pay a flat fee per latent that fires. Loud is fine; showing up is what costs.
cap.2: JumpReLU SAEs penalise L0, the number of active latents, rather than the L1 sum of their sizes. That removes the pressure to shrink, the problem Gated SAEs also attack by a different route.
cap.3: Sparsity via λ·Σᵢ H(zᵢ − θᵢ), trained through the STE, decouples 'whether' from 'how much'. Gated SAEs separate gate from magnitude; JumpReLU uses a learned threshold with a straight-through gradient.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: L0: how many latents fire per token
Load them with SAELens, don't retrain

cap.1: The SAEs you'll load to look inside Gemma use this door. Knowing the bar exists tells you why each latent is either off or clearly on, and what 'L0' counts.
cap.2: Gemma Scope's SAEs are JumpReLU models, loaded with SAELens. L0 is the average number of latents over their threshold per token; the canonical ones were chosen at L0 nearest 100.
cap.3: Thresholds make activations exactly 0 or at least θ, so L0 is crisp and dashboards show clean on/off latents: the vocabulary you'll read, and steer with, in Gemma-based interpretability.

coda.title: Set the bar for eight latents

caption.1: Raise the bar: noisy latents switch off and L0 drops. Flip to classic mode: the same bar also shrinks every survivor. JumpReLU doesn't.
caption.2: Classic mode is soft thresholding, max(z − θ, 0), the pattern an L1 penalty pushes toward: small values cut, θ shaved off big ones. JumpReLU is hard thresholding: cut or keep whole.
caption.3: Soft thresholding is the proximal map of an L1 penalty; hard thresholding is the proximal map of L0. JumpReLU learns a per-latent θ for the hard version, trading a discontinuity for unshrunk magnitudes.

where_else: Gated SAEs: the same shrinkage problem, solved by separating the gate from the magnitude
TopK SAEs: keep exactly k latents per token, another way to control L0 directly
Signal denoising: hard thresholding keeps big coefficients whole, soft thresholding shrinks them

hamming.what: A sparse autoencoder whose latents each have a learned threshold: below it they output zero, above it they pass their full value.
hamming.when: Whenever you load Gemma Scope SAEs, or train an SAE and want sparsity without shrinking the features you keep.
hamming.why: An L1 penalty makes every active latent under-report its strength; a threshold with a count-based penalty cuts noise without shrinking the real signal.

object.title: The cliff-edge ramp
object.subtitle: A ramp that stays flat until the bar, then jumps straight to full height.

cap.1: Across: how strongly a latent wants to fire. Front to back: where its bar is set. Height: what actually comes out.
cap.2: Output of one latent over (pre-activation z, threshold θ) under the JumpReLU gate.
cap.3: f(z, θ) = z·H(z − θ): zero on one side of the diagonal z = θ, equal to z on the other.

cap.1: Look along the diagonal: a sheer cliff. Just below the bar, nothing; just above, the full value.
cap.2: The jump at z = θ is the price of keeping magnitudes whole. Everything past the edge reads its true size.
cap.3: A discontinuity of height θ along z = θ; the exact gradient in θ is zero everywhere off that line.

cap.1: Swap to the classic gate: the cliff becomes a gentle ramp that starts at zero. Everything that gets through has been shaved down.
cap.2: Soft thresholding, max(z − θ, 0), is continuous but subtracts θ from every surviving value: shrinkage in solid form.
cap.3: relu(z − θ) is the L1 proximal map: continuous, biased toward zero by exactly θ on its support.

cap.1: Compare the far edge: the classic sheet sits lower everywhere past the bar. That gap is how much every real feature gets under-reported.
cap.2: At z = 2.8 with θ = 1, JumpReLU reads 2.8 while the soft gate reads 1.8.
cap.3: The bias of the soft gate is exactly θ on its support; the hard gate is unbiased there.

cap.1: From above, the cliff line is where the bar meets the signal. Training slides each latent's bar using a stand-in slope along this edge.
cap.2: The straight-through estimator gives θ a gradient only from inputs landing near the cliff line.
cap.3: The STE's pseudo-gradient is non-zero only in a narrow band around z = θ (its width is the bandwidth), so thresholds learn only from near-threshold pre-activations.

predict.q: A latent's pre-activation is 2.0 and its threshold is 0.5. What does JumpReLU output?
predict.why: Above the bar the value passes through whole. 1.5 is what a shifted ReLU would give.

predict.q: Why can't ordinary backprop learn the threshold?

options.t: The step has zero slope almost everywhere
The threshold is not a parameter
It would make the SAE dense

predict.why: Nudging θ changes nothing until it crosses a value. The straight-through estimator supplies a stand-in gradient near the bar.

predict.q: Compared with an L1 penalty, what does counting active latents (L0) avoid?

options.t: Shrinking the latents that do fire

predict.why: L1 charges by size, so it pushes every active value down. L0 charges by count, so size is free.

object.where: Anywhere a signal should be either off or fully on: hard thresholding in signal denoising and sparse coding.
